newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chocolate firms cautious for 1997.
newsitem.headline: German chocolate firms cautious for 1997.

text.p: Tight domestic consumer budgets and less accessible export markets in eastern Europe are clouding modest growth prospects in Germany's chocolate industry, trade and manufacturing sources said.
"Domestic markets should consolidate in 1997 while growth hopes focus on exports, where the weaker mark may help," said Nikolaus Reingen of confectionery industry association BDS.
"Eastern European buyers are ordering lower volumes but they are seeking higher value products."
Reingen, foreign trade manager at BDS, spoke following the annual confectionery trade fair ISM in Cologne on January 26-30.
Participants said the ISM, which has become more of a showcase for product innovations than a forum for sales, helped underpin sentiment, but did not create any euphoria.
"Exhibitors are not unhappy and they are confident of better exports, but companies have realised the domestic market cannot grow," a cocoa trader said.
"It's hard to gauge likely cocoa use from the results of a finished product show, but I would not expect a higher rate of cocoa consumption by the industry in 1997," he said.
Germany's cocoa grind, a chocolate consumption indicator, dropped by three percent to 251,069 tonnes last year.

Domestic chocolate and boiled sweets sales last year were up one percent from 1995 at 2.44 million tonnes while sales values should have stagnated at 1995's 18.00 billion marks, according to figures published by BDS.
Per-capita chocolate consumption stands at 8.44 kg.
Only expanionist market leaders are optimistic.
"We have operated very positively in a stagnating market," said a spokeswoman for the German Mars GmbH company in Viersen.
Mars, which raised 1996 sales by 10 percent to 900 million marks, supported its chocolate bar sales with 100 million marks of advertising, 25 percent more than in 1995.
It has launched a new cereals bar to complement its classic chocolate bar range, where it is the market leader in sales outlets such as kiosks and petrol stations.
A spokesman for Nestle Chocoladen GmbH, part of Nestle Deutschland AG, said "Growth won't come from a rise in demand but from the success of product innovations."

Nestle Chocoladen reported 1996 net sales of 858 million marks, 4.1 percent more than in 1995. Profits were not reported but were expected to reflect high advertising spending and a competitive retail price structure.
Advertising will cost 80 million marks this year.
Nestle will newly introduce a new dairy snack bar as well as a peanut butter bar already successful in the U.S.
At Ritter GmbH & Co KG, which raised its market share in 100-gram chocolate bars wo percent to 20 percent on 1996 sales of 470 million marks, advertising cost 50 million marks.

Small and medium sized firms complain that growth among market leaders is at the cost of mergers and company failures while forays made by multi-nationals into eastern Europe means they can no longer export finished products.
BDS said Eastern European trade barriers also limit German access. Exporters said new demands for native language lists of ingredients were one example of such moves to curtail imports.
